extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media analysts, journalism students, and practicing journalists interested in news production and framing
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and production guidance about how news organizations and journalistic practices frame, select, and report on social movements and related public issues. Emphasizes institutional, professional, and linguistic factors shaping coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-oriented reporting / reporters adopt source outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters tend, over time, to adopt the outlook of the news sources with whom they are associated: They ask the questions appropriate to their sources' world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions contain their own answers and thus guide where reporters look and what they find; reporters' alignment with sources reconstitutes both topic and a 'world' for coverage. Example: reporters unused to a beat notice different aspects of events (Nixon Thanksgiving example). Anti-pattern: treating reporters as neutral observers without accounting for source-driven question framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalization limits radical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The successful institutionalization of a social movement can limit its ability to carry forth radical issues because canons of neutrality lead journalists to 'balance' movement views against opposing organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As movements institutionalize (central offices, lobbying), media apply neutrality and balance norms that can neutralize or reframe radical claims; coverage therefore shifts toward debate-format rather than accepting the movement's systemic analyses as factual. Scoring note: institutionalized movements are more likely to be covered in routinized, depoliticized terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement/segregation of coverage (women's page vs. general pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of news about a movement on segregated pages (e.g., women's page) classifies those stories among food, fashions, and furnishings rather than 'pressing affairs of the day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement signals audience and importance, telling some readers (e.g., men) that those issues are not their concern. Debated tactic: proponents argue advantages to specialized placement while critics say segregation marginalizes issues. Practical implication: where editors assign a story affects public perception and political salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat assignment subjects movements to the conventional news narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: When issues become the responsibility of beat and general reporters, they are subjected to the frame of the conventional news narrative and cannot propound leaders' structural analyses as factual statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories must center on who, what, where, and the mechanics of why/how; leaders' analyses are reduced to practical recommendations subject to juxtaposed refutation. Result: movements cannot undercut the news 'web of facticity.' Example: movement claims about systemic causes are treated as opinion or prompted controversy rather than factual exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft consciousness: concrete logic and present-time orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic 'craft consciousness' entails 'the logic of the concrete, a present time orientation, and an emphasis on contingent events rather than structural necessities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This professional habit discourages linking events to broader structures (e.g., connecting inflation to war), favoring immediate, exemplified incidents. Anti-pattern: journalists parodying structural analyses (e.g., linguistic sexism arguments) rather than engaging analytically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facticity and professional objectivity (fairness through methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only must newsworkers be factual, but facts must also be fair: by balancing opinions of newsmakers and weighing evidence, newsworkers strive for a fair presentation of the facts to inform the public and maintain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional methods that claim to secure fairness include gathering supplementary evidence, presenting conflicting truth-claims, using quotation marks, and leveraging procedural familiarity (e.g., police routines). These methods function as the news media's way to 'reveal social reality' and to justify crusades only insofar as they adhere to 'fairness.' Scoring: evaluate whether coverage uses these methods to support claims of objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation and labeling of economic/corporate news
rubrics_metrics.description: News about the corporate sector is often segregated as 'financial news' and treated separately from general news, with special visual/sectional signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segregation masks interconnections between government and corporate activity; only when government intervenes visibly does economic news move into general (nonanalytic) frames. Practical effect: readers are less likely to perceive structural ties between public policy and corporate power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining an artificial public/private distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: By maintaining an artificial distinction between public and private, the news media mask the actual organization of significant services and the intertwinement of state and corporate interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic tendencies to report on public institutions more readily than powerful private ones—even when private entities receive public funds—obscure accountability and limit analytic understanding. Example: criticizing municipal universities but not private institutions that receive public money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and metaphor choices that obscure structural realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic practices—e.g., referring to the corporate sector as 'big business' rather than 'corporate capitalism' or 'monopoly capitalism'—reinforce older, less analytic images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such lexical choices invoke competitive-market imagery instead of revealing concentration, conglomeration, and state-corporate ties. Evaluate reportage for vocabulary that sanitizes structures and limits possible analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over access and ownership shapes whose 'right to know' prevails
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are private property and owners/publishers have the legal right to publish what they will; publishers are not legally required to grant access to anyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access control (ownership, licensing) is crucial to whose ideas reach the public and thus to what counts as truth; legal distinctions (newspaper ownership vs. electronic licenses) complicate First Amendment issues. Practical implication: assess how ownership and access policies limit or enable voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: News frames legitimize the status quo and contain dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass media limit the frames within which public issues are debated and thus narrow available political alternatives; dissenting opinions are often presented as curious heresies or irrelevant eccentricities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage practices can foster a 'climate of conformity' by containing dissent within marginal frames rather than engaging it analytically. Example: dissenters treated as 'of no consequence' rather than substantive challengers. Evaluate whether reporting marginalizes or integrates dissenting perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter demographics and professional networks limit visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' social class and professional networks (e.g., middle-class feminist journalists) shape what they see and therefore write about, making some movement components more visible than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure primarily to colleagues and professional friends can bias coverage toward certain groups (e.g., white middle class) while obscuring black, Puerto Rican, and working-class activists. Scoring note: measure diversity of sources and visible constituencies in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratization redirects movement toward politics and law
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaucratic establishment of central offices facilitates beat reporting but helps redirect social movements from consciousness-raising to electoral politics and legal lobbying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As movements institutionalize (e.g., National Women's Political Caucus located in Washington), issues become the province of political, education, court, or labor reporters rather than pages dedicated to movement consciousness, changing story frames and practical emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial power to exclude or sanitize news
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and news organizations exercise power to exclude occurrences or to edit material in ways that can 'rescue' subjects (e.g., editing out critical observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to include, exclude, or edit particular details (e.g., omitting a president's shaking hands) impacts public understanding; assess editorial interventions and their effects on accountability and narrative balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signed columns vs. general news: distinct norms for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Signed political columns explicitly acknowledge constructed interpretation, whereas general news distinguishes its constructedness by emphasizing facticity and neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional separation allows news organizations to present analysis and opinion in marked venues while preserving the appearance of neutral factual reporting in news pages; evaluate whether analyses are properly labeled and whether 'news' conceals interpretive work.
